Oriented from `13bdfc2` (own prior pass: `generate_cv.py`'s own `_footer()` was the one genuine gap left in the control-character-guard bug class, now exhausted). `git fetch`/`merge --ff-only` confirmed clean - still at `13bdfc2`, no new commits, no collision. Open PRs re-checked: only `#164`/`#165` remain (both untouched since 2026-10-26). Backlog cross-checked against the recent chain: 19 total, 3 genuinely open (`start_payfast_checkout()`'s revenue gap, the impersonation session-refresh gap, `held_registrations`-vs-CV) - self-consistent, none touched this pass.

With the control-character bug class now closed and the discovery-scraper live-test rotation's next candidates (`lephalale.py`/`vaal_central_water.py`/`capetown_procurement.py`/`kouga.py`) still queued for a future pass, re-examined this session's own just-fixed TOCTOU-race family (0113/0114/0115/0116) for a sibling instance, rather than assuming it's now exhausted everywhere a check-then-insert shape appears. Found one in `app/tenders/[id]/actions.ts`'s `requestSubmissionPack()`: a plain `SELECT ... from pack_generation_jobs where tender_id = ... and status in ('requested','generating') limit 1` (line ~155) gates a friendly "A submission pack is already queued for this tender." rejection, well before the function's one real write - the `request_submission_pack_checked()` RPC (0115) - runs. 0115 already locks `company_subscriptions` for the company-wide quota check, but that lock (and that function) says nothing about a second request for the exact same tender; the only thing stopping a true duplicate is `pack_generation_jobs_one_open_key` (0026), a unique index on `(company_id, tender_id, engine, kind) where status in ('requested','generating')` - and `request_submission_pack_checked()`'s insert has no `on conflict`/exception handling around it, unlike its sibling `request_general_job_checked()` in the same migration (which deliberately uses `on conflict do nothing`).

So the race window is real: two requests for the SAME tender close enough together (a double-click, two tabs, a slow-network retry) can both pass the plain SELECT before either's RPC call commits - the first's insert succeeds, the second's hits the unique index and raises a raw `23505`, which `requestSubmissionPack()`'s own error handling (`fail(error.message || "Could not request...")`) would show to the user verbatim - the exact "raw constraint-violation string leaks to the user instead of the friendly message the happy path already has" shape `redeem_company_invite()` was fixed for in `0116`, just one call site over.

Reproduced directly in a disposable scratch database (`engine/security/replay_schema.sh`, `postgresql` service started first since this is a fresh container): one company (active, 5 packs/month - comfortably under quota, isolating this from 0115's own already-fixed quota race), one tender, one `tender_packs` row. Called `request_submission_pack_checked()` for that tender twice in direct succession (sequential calls are enough to prove this - the race lives in the TypeScript-side window between the SELECT and the RPC call, not inside the RPC's own locking, which was never meant to cover this check). First call: succeeded, returned a job id. Second call, same tender: raised `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "pack_generation_jobs_one_open_key"` with the real company/tender UUIDs in `DETAIL` - confirmed the exact raw string that would otherwise reach the user.

Fixed the same way `requestTenderCv()` already handles the identical shape for `generated_cvs` (0075) in this exact same file - no migration needed, since the unique index (0026) already fully prevents the actual duplicate row; only the error message needed fixing. Added `if (error.code === "23505")` before the generic `error.message` fallback in `requestSubmissionPack()`'s own error handling, mapping it to the same friendly message the plain-SELECT happy path already shows ("A submission pack is already queued for this tender.").

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` on the full `app/` project - `0` errors. `npx eslint "app/tenders/[id]/actions.ts"` - clean, no new findings. Re-ran the same two-calls-same-tender scratch-DB scenario mentally against the new code path (the fix is pure TypeScript error-mapping, not a SQL change, so the scratch-DB repro above - proving the RPC really does raise `23505` on this exact race - is the correct and sufficient verification; no separate red-then-green test file exists for this, matching this codebase's own convention that Server Actions calling Supabase directly aren't unit-tested here - `requestTenderCv()`'s own identical 23505 catch two lines above has none either).

**Backlog: 19, unchanged** - standalone bug, fixed; not a new judgment-call item. `held_registrations`-vs-CV, `start_payfast_checkout()`'s revenue gap, and the impersonation session-refresh gap all untouched, as directed.

Oriented from `e7ce44a` (own prior pass: `transnet_etenders.py` re-tested live, genuinely clean). `git fetch`/`merge --ff-only` confirmed clean, no new commits, no collision. Continued the discovery-scraper live-test rotation `13f3f4d` (Eskom) and `e7ce44a` (Transnet) both used: `sars_procurement.py`, `lephalale.py`, `vaal_central_water.py`, `capetown_procurement.py`, `kouga.py` were all still last live-tested 2026-11-01. Picked `sars_procurement.py`.

Ran it live: 2 real open tenders. Both had `closing_date: None` - traced why rather than assuming it was a transient scrape miss. `normalize()` has never set `closing_date` at all (confirmed via `git log` on the file: the original "Add 3 new discovery sources" commit never included it, and nothing since has either) - only `published_date` is extracted. Checked the real live page's raw HTML directly rather than assuming the source genuinely has no closing date to give: it does - a separate "Published Tenders" detail section (distinct from the dated `<ul>` "What's New" summary list `parse_listing()` already reads) states `Closing Date: DD/MM/YYYY HH:MM` for each tender, right next to its title (confirmed live: `RFP14/2026` -> `17/11/2026 11:00`, `RFP18/2026` -> `10/11/2026 11:00`). Every SARS tender this source has ever discovered has been missing its real closing date entirely - no deadline countdown, no "closing soon" flag, nothing.

Fixed by adding `_closing_dates_by_ref()`, keying each detail block's stated closing date by its parsed RFP reference, and attaching it in `parse_listing()`/`normalize()`. Deliberately NOT routed through `source_http.parse_sast()`'s own ambiguous US-style (month-first) slash-date branch - SARS's format is day-first, and a day/month both <=12 (a real, common case) would silently transpose under that reading; the day/month/year are parsed explicitly and handed to `sh.iso_sast()` only as an unambiguous ISO string instead.

Caught and fixed a real bug in my own first version of the fix before it reached main: the first regex used an unbounded `.*?` between `<strong>title</strong>` and `Closing Date:`, which crossed over unrelated `<strong>` tags earlier on the page (the "What's New" summary list's own date headings) and attached the wrong date - caught by my own new test (deliberately ordered the fixture's summary section before its detail section, the opposite of the real page's own order, specifically to catch this), not by luck matching the live page's current ordering. Fixed with a `(?:(?!<strong>).)*?` bound that refuses to cross into another `<strong>` block.

Verified for real: re-ran against the real live site after the fix - `RFP14/2026` -> `2026-11-17T11:00:00+02:00`, `RFP18/2026` -> `2026-11-10T11:00:00+02:00`, matching the page exactly. Added 2 new assertions to `test_gov_sources.py` (closing-date extraction with the day/month-both-<=12 safety case spelled out explicitly; a tender with no stated closing date still parses to `None`, not a crash) - full suite `ALL PASSED`. `ast.parse` clean; `ruff check` - all findings pre-existing or matching the file's own existing `re.S` convention (`DATE_BLOCK` above already uses the identical style), none newly introduced.

## This pass (2026-11-05, standing solution-architect review): fixed - `dispatchTriage.ts`'s `operationalStatusMessage()` stayed silent on a digital submission `classifyDispatchBucket()` already classified "critical", because only the physical-box path computed an urgency deadline

Oriented from `8ba8a2b` (own prior pass: the double-click quota investigation). `git fetch`/
`merge --ff-only` picked up `1f15ad9` (a sibling pass: intake rotation re-confirmed exhausted, no new
bug) - no collision. Open PRs re-checked: only `#164`/`#165` remain (both untouched since 2026-10-26).
Backlog chain re-confirmed: 19 total, 3 genuinely open.

This deep into the session almost every obvious area has had a dedicated pass. Grepped
`System-Status.md`'s own history for mention counts across `app/app/`/`engine/` file names to find a
genuinely light corner: the Tender Command Center's submission-logistics feature (migration `0090`,
`lib/dispatchTriage.ts`) had only passing mentions, never its own pass. Read the module end to end -
it's carefully written, with an unusually explicit header comment about what it deliberately does
NOT try to derive and why (no second, drift-prone copy of `blocking_items`/`decision_needed`).

**Found a real, reachable inconsistency between two sibling functions in the same file.**
`classifyDispatchBucket()` has an explicit digital-submission fallback: when `printSignDeadline()` is
null (submission type isn't `physical_box`, so there's no print/transit buffer to compute), it falls
back to the closing date itself for the same 48-hour urgency window, so an eTenders-portal upload
closing soon still lands in the dashboard's Critical lane. `operationalStatusMessage()` - the same
module's "system speaks to you" status line, called from the real tender workspace page
(`app/app/tenders/[id]/page.tsx`, confirmed by grep, not assumed) - has no equivalent fallback: it
only ever computes `deadline`/`hoursLeft` from `printSignDeadline()`, which is always null for a
digital submission. The result: a tender genuinely bucketed "critical" could have its own status
line say nothing urgent at all, or show an unrelated blocking summary with no mention of the real
48-hour deadline.

**Verified directly, not assumed**: ran both functions against the identical input (an `etenders_
portal` tender closing in 20 hours, not yet dispatched) - `classifyDispatchBucket()` correctly
returned `"critical"`; `operationalStatusMessage()` returned `null`.

**Fixed** by adding the same digital-submission fallback to `operationalStatusMessage()`, mirroring
`classifyDispatchBucket()`'s own 48-hour window and `notYetDispatched` guard exactly (reusing the
same `DISPATCHED_STATUSES` constant already in the module) - closing-based wording ("until closing")
rather than print-cutoff wording, since a digital submission has no print step, plus a new
`"SUBMISSION OVERDUE"` message mirroring the existing `"PRINT OVERDUE"` one for the past-closing case.

**Verified for real**: manually ran 5 scenarios directly against the fixed functions (critical with
no blocking summary, critical with one, overdue, already-dispatched inside the window - correctly
stays silent, outside the 48h window - correctly stays silent) before writing tests. Added 4 new
tests to `dispatchTriage.test.ts` covering the same scenarios. `git stash` of just the source fix
(keeping the new tests) confirmed genuine red - 2/28 failing - then genuine green restored, 28/28.
Full regression `node --experimental-strip-types --test lib/*.test.ts`: 226/226 (was 222, +4 new),
unaffected. `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` both clean on both touched files.

**Reproduced directly in a disposable scratch database** (106 migrations replayed, dropped after
use): seeded a trialing company, called `request_general_job_checked()` once for a tender (succeeds,

pre-existing, unchanged. Called `company_can_request_pack()` directly against the identical seeded
state (the exact function the pre-0115 TypeScript called before ever reaching its own separate
insert): it already returns `false` here too. The quota gate has never distinguished "this in-flight
job is for the SAME tender I'm now re-requesting" from "this in-flight job is for a different one" -
that's true of `0084`'s original in-flight-counting fix, `0096`'s trial-lapse layer, and `0115`'s
re-merge of both; `0115` didn't introduce this interaction, it faithfully preserved behaviour that
already existed. The `on conflict do nothing` path's real, working purpose is the different scenario
it was actually built for - an ACTIVE company comfortably under its monthly quota hitting a genuine
double-click race, where the quota check still passes on the second call and the unique index/
on-conflict-do-nothing correctly prevents a duplicate row, silently. Not independently re-verified
with its own scratch-DB reproduction this pass (already covered conceptually by `9d43a72`'s broader
"the atomic lock pattern works as designed" verification) - the trial-cap case above was the one
genuinely worth tracing, since it's the one where the "silent no-op" promise could plausibly fail.

## This pass (2026-11-04, standing solution-architect review): fixed - `create_company_and_join()` had an unguarded TOCTOU race that could give one user two companies, which every single page in the app assumes can't happen

Oriented from `6e08b0c` (own prior pass: Market Intelligence's bidder-count gate). `git fetch`/`merge
--ff-only` picked up `4303fb9` (a sibling pass: the claim-outside-try-block isolation gap swept across
all four remaining bridges) - no collision, no duplication. Open PRs re-checked: only `#164`/`#165`
remain (both untouched since 2026-10-26).

Cross-checked the backlog chain and the corrected "10 pending migrations" figure again (now a standing
discipline): self-consistent, 19 unchanged, `ls app/supabase/migrations/ | grep -E
"^(0096|0107|0108|0109|0110|0111|0112|0113|0114|0115)_"` still returns 10.

Directed to the onboarding flow or notifications/digest. Read `app/app/onboarding/` end to end
(`page.tsx`, `actions.ts`, `Step1.tsx`, `AddDocumentsScreen.tsx`, `WizardShell.tsx`, `fields.tsx`) -
the 2026-10-31 clean sweep of this area still holds, nothing new in the UI layer itself. Pivoted to the
one privileged write it depends on, `create_company_and_join()` (0003), since that function's own
read/write shape had never specifically been checked for the TOCTOU pattern this session has now found
three times elsewhere (`createInvite`'s seat cap, `team/actions.ts`'s last-owner check,
`company_can_request_pack()`'s quota).

**Found**: `create_company_and_join()` checks "does this user already belong to a company" (`exists
(select 1 from company_members where user_id = auth.uid())`) and inserts the new `company_members` row
as two steps in the same function, with nothing locking between them. `company_members` has no unique
constraint on `user_id` alone (only the composite `unique(company_id, user_id)` from `0001`), so two
concurrent calls for the SAME new user (a double-click on Screen 1's "Continue" button, or a slow-
network retry) can both pass the check before either commits, both insert - one user ends up owning TWO
real companies. This is worse than the other three races: grepped every page that reads a user's own
company (`AppShell.tsx`, `/billing`, `/experience`, `/my-cv`, `/onboarding` itself,
`company/officeActions.ts`) and all seven call `.eq("user_id", ...).maybeSingle()` - PostgREST's
`.maybeSingle()` errors the moment more than one row matches, so a user caught by this race gets a hard
error on every single page in the app from then on, not just onboarding.

**Reproduced directly** in a disposable scratch database (never the live DB): one real `auth.users`
row, two concurrent `create_company_and_join()` calls for that same user - both succeeded, returning two
different company ids; `select count(*) from company_members where user_id = ...` confirmed 2 rows, both
`role = 'owner'`.

**Fixed** with migration `0116`: `alter table company_members add constraint
company_members_user_id_key unique (user_id)`. Not a SECURITY DEFINER + `for update` rewrite like
0113/0114/0115 - there's no pre-existing row to lock on for a brand-new user, and the table's own 0001
comment already states "v1 has one company" per the product while every read site above already
hard-assumes it, so this formalizes an invariant the whole app already depends on rather than
introducing a new one. A concurrent second insert now blocks on the unique index until the first
commits, then fails with a 23505 instead of succeeding; because the whole function runs in one
transaction, the losing call's own `companies` insert rolls back too - no orphaned, member-less company
row left behind.

While adding the constraint, found the exact same "join a second company" path already existed, un-
raced, in `redeem_company_invite()` (0107): a user already in company A accepting an invite to company
B previously succeeded silently as a second `company_members` row - already a live landmine against the
same universal `.maybeSingle()` assumption, just reached a different way. The new constraint alone would
have turned that into a raw `duplicate key value violates unique constraint` string leaking straight to
`app/invite/actions.ts`'s `acceptInvite()`, which redirects with `error.message` shown as-is - so
`0116` also re-creates `redeem_company_invite()` with one added check before the insert, raising a
friendly, specific message instead. Redeeming an invite for the SAME company (re-opening an old link, a
role change) is unaffected - still the existing on-conflict-update-role path, unchanged.

**Verified for real**: replayed all 106 migrations (including `0116`) on a fresh scratch database -
clean. Re-ran the identical two-concurrent-calls scenario against the fix: first call succeeds, second
blocks on the lock then fails with the unique-constraint error, exactly 1 `company_members` row results,
and the loser's own `companies` row count for that test confirmed 0 (no orphan). Separately tested
`redeem_company_invite()`'s new guard directly: a user already owning company A, invited to company B,
gets the friendly "You already belong to a different company..." message (not a raw constraint string);
re-tested the SAME-company re-redemption path (re-opening an old invite link) immediately after and
confirmed it still works unchanged - role updated via the existing `on conflict` clause. No TypeScript
changed - both `createCompanyBasics()` and `acceptInvite()` already handle any RPC error generically, so
no app-code change was needed either side. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean (sanity check only, nothing touched).
Full regression `node --experimental-strip-types --test app/lib/*.test.ts` - 222/222, unaffected (as
expected, no TS touched). Three scratch databases created and dropped immediately after each check,
never the live DB.

**Backlog: 19, unchanged** (standalone bug, fixed - not a new judgment-call item; 11 pending migrations
now `0096`/`0107`-`0116`, the `held_registrations`-vs-CV judgment call, the `start_payfast_checkout()`
revenue-integrity gap, and the impersonation session-refresh gap all still open, needing Sarel's own
call. None of those three touched this pass, as directed.)

`app/app/tenders/[id]/market-context.tsx`'s own "real market, not just this tender" panel). Found: the

sub-metric (`pct_of_estimate_n`) but never to the bidder-count sub-metric (`bidder_count_n`), even though

stop, we never guess" principle the sibling metric already enforces, and that this file's own test suite

- `proxy.ts`'s own route-guarding logic (redirect-to-login, redirect-to-onboarding) is unaffected by
  this - it always authenticates against the admin's own real session, by design, never the
  impersonation overlay - so this is specifically and only about the impersonated session silently
  dying mid-use, not a route-guard bug.

pair captured and re-persisted into the `tt_impersonation` cookie from `proxy.ts` (the one place that

generate_cv.py`, `engine/sanral_fill.py`, `engine/make_envelope_covers.py` - the only 4 files that

comment only discusses openpyxl, never calls it; `sanral_fill.py` explicitly avoids it). Bug class
genuinely exhausted - moved to a fresh area per the standing instruction to rotate once a class is
closed out.

Picked billing/subscription logic beyond invites and the PayFast ITN handler itself (plan upgrade/
downgrade, never given a dedicated pass this session) and read `/api/billing/checkout/route.ts` and
`start_payfast_checkout()` (0078/0083) end to end. Found something serious, not a code-shape bug like
this session's recent run of fixes but a real design gap with direct revenue impact:

`GET /api/billing/checkout` - hit the instant a signed-in user clicks "Upgrade"/"Downgrade"/"Subscribe"
on `/billing`, **before** any redirect to PayFast and before any payment - calls `start_payfast_checkout
(p_plan_tier, p_billing_interval)`, which immediately `UPDATE`s `company_subscriptions` to the NEW
plan's `plan_tier`/`billing_interval`/`max_users`/`max_packs_per_month` (0083's `tt_plan_limits()`).
`status` and `current_period_end` are deliberately left untouched by this call - by design, so a
currently-'active' subscriber mid-upgrade keeps showing as paid-up while PayFast processes the real
charge. But nothing ever reverts the plan/limits change if that charge never actually completes:
- If the user simply never finishes the PayFast page (closes the tab, no ITN of any kind is ever
  sent by PayFast for a transaction nobody submitted) - `company_subscriptions` is left permanently on
  the new, higher plan's seats/packs, `status` still `'active'`, `current_period_end` still the OLD
  (already-paid-for) date. Nothing re-checks this later. No reconciliation job exists (same absence as
  the already-flagged Finding 97, a *different* gap about `current_period_end` lapsing silently).
- Even if PayFast DOES send a `FAILED` ITN (a declined card), `apply_payfast_itn()`'s own normal path
  (0078/0083/0110/0112) sets `status = 'past_due'` but still never reverts `plan_tier`/`max_users`/
  `max_packs_per_month` - and `lib/billing.ts`'s own header comment confirms `past_due` is "a banner,
  not a silent lock-out," so the user keeps full access at the new plan's limits regardless.

**Reproduced directly** against a disposable scratch Postgres (103 migrations replayed clean, dropped
immediately after): seeded a company `active` on Professional (`max_users=5`, `max_packs_per_month=15`,
`current_period_end` 20 days out), called `start_payfast_checkout('business', 'monthly')` as that
company's owner with no ITN ever following it - `company_subscriptions` immediately read back
`plan_tier='business'`, `max_users=10`, `max_packs_per_month=30`, `status` still `'active'`,
`current_period_end` completely unchanged (still the old Professional period). A real, free, repeatable
self-upgrade with zero payment confirmation, exploitable by any existing active subscriber simply by
visiting the checkout link and abandoning it - not a contrived edge case.

**Not fixed - a genuine design/judgment call, not a safe one-line patch.** The architecture already
knows the right pattern for this exact situation: `apply_payfast_itn()`'s own "rescue" path (0081/0082,
used when a LATER checkout attempt has superseded an earlier `m_payment_id` on `company_subscriptions`)
deliberately does NOT trust whatever plan the row currently shows - it reads the plan the payment
attempt itself was for, from the append-only `payfast_payment_attempts` log, and only grants it on a
confirmed `COMPLETE` ITN. The "normal" (non-superseded) path is the one place that discipline was
never applied - it trusts `company_subscriptions.plan_tier` was already set correctly by checkout,
because historically checkout and the eventual ITN were for the SAME still-current `m_payment_id`, with
no notion of "this plan change hasn't been confirmed yet." Fixing this properly needs a real decision:
whether to defer the plan/limit change until a confirmed `COMPLETE` ITN (mirroring the rescue path, but
for the not-yet-superseded case too - a bigger behavior change than it sounds, since it also changes
what the UI shows immediately after someone clicks "Upgrade"), add an explicit `pending_plan_tier`/
`pending_billing_interval` column pair and a UI treatment for it, or add a reconciliation sweep that
reverts an unconfirmed plan change after some grace window. Flagging for Sarel's own call, not guessing
at UX/product intent for money-adjacent state.

has two separate callers and stays an open, unfixed judgment call.

`createInvite()` enforced a plan's seat cap (`max_users`, 0083) with three separate client queries -
select `max_users`, count `company_members` + pending `company_invites`, compare, then insert - no
lock between the count and the insert. **Reproduced the race directly** in a disposable scratch
database (not this app's live DB, dropped immediately after): a company with `max_users=2` and 1
existing member (room for exactly 1 more), the old three-query shape run from two concurrent `psql`
sessions with a `pg_sleep` between the count and the insert to widen the window - both sessions read
count=1 (under the cap), both passed the check, both inserted. Result: 2 pending invites against a
company that already had its 1 remaining seat - the real bug, not assumed from reading the code.

`create_company_invite_checked()` that does the whole check-then-insert inside one transaction, with

0107 already proved for `redeem_company_invite()`). Also checks `tt_is_company_admin()` (0050) and
reads `invited_by` from `auth.uid()` directly rather than a caller-supplied parameter - this function
is granted to `authenticated` and therefore callable directly via `supabase.rpc()`, not only through
this app's own Server Action, so it can't rely on the action's own admin check being the only caller
(the same "never trust a parameter for identity, never assume the SQL function has only one caller"
convention this session's SECURITY DEFINER audits already established). `createInvite()` now calls
this one RPC instead of three separate queries.

**Re-ran the exact same concurrency test against the fix**: same starting state (1 member, room for 1
more), two concurrent `create_company_invite_checked()` calls - the first succeeded (returned a real
new invite id), the second blocked on the lock until the first committed, then correctly saw the seat
as taken and raised `P0004` ("Your plan allows 2 people...") instead of inserting. Exactly 1 pending
invite resulted, matching the real 1 free seat - not 2.

## This pass (2026-11-03, standing solution-architect review): checked whether `caa5148`'s "one malformed row crashes the whole parse" shape recurs on any other discovery scraper - genuinely clean, no second instance found

Oriented from `caa5148` (a sibling pass: `list_tenders.py`'s `_parse_row()` unpacked exactly 6 values
from a SANRAL AJAX row with no guard against a shorter row - one malformed row crashed
`fetch_tenders()`'s own unguarded list comprehension, losing every OTHER real tender in that same
response too, not just the bad one; fixed with a per-row try/except). That bug's real shape is
specific: a `normalize()`/`_parse_row()` call inside an unguarded list comprehension, fed from a row
structure whose required field(s) can genuinely be absent - not "any parsing code could theoretically
throw," which is true everywhere and not actionable on its own.

Checked every discovery scraper with the same `[normalize(...) for r in rows]` shape
(`cidb_tenders.py`, `dbsa_procurement.py`, `etenders_national.py`, `etenders_portal.py`,
`award_outcomes.py`, `capetown_procurement.py`, `kouga.py`, `randwater.py`,
`vaal_central_water.py`) for the same two ingredients SANRAL's bug needed: (1) a `normalize()` that
indexes a required field directly (`row['x']`, not `row.get('x')`) and (2) a realistic path for that
field to be missing by the time `normalize()` sees the row. Found:

- `cidb_tenders.py`, `etenders_national.py`, `award_outcomes.py`'s `normalize_portal_award()`: every
  field read via `.get()` throughout - a missing field becomes `None` in the output, never a crash.
- `kouga.py`, `randwater.py`, `vaal_central_water.py`: rows are fixed-arity tuples built directly from
  a regex's own fixed capture-group count (`CARD_RE.findall()`, `BID_BLOCK.findall()`,
  `ROW_FIELDS.search()` unpacked once per row) - a regex match can never return the wrong number of
  groups, so the arity SANRAL's bug depended on (a JSON array row with fewer cells than expected)
  structurally cannot happen here.
- `capetown_procurement.py`'s `normalize_rfq(cells, path, detail_id)` reads `cells[0..2]` directly,
  but the call site (`... for row in parse_table(page) if len(row[0]) >= 4`) already guards the
  length before calling it - confirmed by reading the actual filter, not assumed from the function
  name.
- `dbsa_procurement.py`'s `normalize(row)` reads `row['ref']`/`row['title']`/`row['closing']`/
  `row['published']`/`row['documents']` by direct index, not `.get()` - looked the most SANRAL-shaped
  at first glance. But `parse_table()` (this module's own row builder) always constructs all 5 keys on
  every row it emits, `published`/`closing` included as `None` when the source cell count is short,
  never omitted - so the KeyError this shape could otherwise raise is not reachable from this module's
  own data.
- `etenders_portal.py`'s `normalize(row, status_hint)` reads `row['id']` directly (twice) - the one
  real near-miss. But `dedupe_rows()` (the function's only real caller's own pre-filter,
  `rels = [normalize(r, status) for r in dedupe_rows(rows)]`) already does `i = r.get("id"); if i is
  None: continue` before any row reaches `normalize()` - every surviving row is guaranteed to have a
  non-`None` id by construction. Confirmed by reading `dedupe_rows()`'s actual body, not inferred.

No second instance of `caa5148`'s bug class found. No code change this pass - a genuinely checked
negative result, not a skipped check.

**Backlog: 20 → 20** (7 pending migrations `0096`, `0107`-`0112`; the `held_registrations`-vs-CV
judgment call from the 2026-11-03 14:16 entry - nothing added or resolved this pass).

(`git merge --ff-only`) before trusting anything, per the standing reminder from two passes ago. Open
PRs re-checked: only `#164`/`#165`, both unchanged since 2026-10-26, no collision.

Every productive bug-class sweep this session (field-stored-but-never-shown, zip/PDF/XML decompression
bombs, job-claim TOCTOU, SECURITY DEFINER ownership checks, the 5 real LLM call sites, the
`briefing_shortlisted` allow-list thread) is now explicitly marked exhausted in this doc's own recent

**Closed that out for real.** Built actual adversarial strings and timed the two most quantifier-heavy
patterns found:
- `capetown_procurement.py`'s `re.sub(r"(\|\s*)+", "|", flat)`: ran against 2000 repetitions of
  `"|" + 50 spaces` with no closing match, and against a single 2000-char whitespace run after one

constant multiplier, not exponential) or anchored by a literal that fixes where each repetition must

`narrative`): every one does a single atomic `PATCH .../table?id=eq.X&status=eq.requested` (confirmed
by reading `SupabaseRest.update()`'s/`supabase_request()`'s own query-string construction in each
file - the status filter is applied server-side, in the same statement as the write, by PostgREST/
Postgres, never a separate SELECT-then-UPDATE from Python) - `process_pack_jobs.py:672`'s own
`client.update(..., {"id": job["id"], "status": "requested"}, {"status": "generating", ...})` and the
near-identical pattern in the other four. An empty result means another worker already won the race;
nothing here can double-claim. Genuinely exhausted, not a new finding.

**2. Regex catastrophic backtracking / ReDoS.** Grepped `engine/` for the classic vulnerable shape
(nested quantifiers over the same/overlapping character class, e.g. `(\s*)+`, `(.+)+`). Found 5
candidates with a nested-quantifier *shape* (`score_outlook.py`, `capetown_procurement.py`,
`key_person_minimums.py`, `vaal_central_water.py`, `fill_flat_pdf.py`) but none has the actual
ambiguity ReDoS needs - each inner quantifier is anchored by a distinguishing literal (a specific
word, a literal `|`, a literal `\s` boundary) that fixes where each repetition must start, so there's
no way for the engine to try multiple overlapping splits of the same substring. Did not attempt to
exhaustively prove safety the way the two decompression-bomb passes did (no real pathological input
built and timed against any of these five) - this is a documented, honest "nothing found by
inspection," not a "confirmed safe by test" result like those two passes. Worth a future pass
actually timing these five against adversarial input if more rigor is wanted; not escalating it as a
backlog item since inspection alone is enough to say nothing need change today.

**3. Upload-filename-sanitizer consistency - found and fixed.** `app/lib/safeFileName.ts`'s own
header comment (written when it was extracted) warned that "~8 other action files hand-rolled their
own narrower inline version... not exploitable today... but one future edit... would reopen path
traversal in just that file, with no shared place to fix it." Grepped every upload action file left
in `app/app` for that exact inline pattern (`replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9._-]/g, "_")`) rather than trusting
the stale "~8" count: all but one have since been migrated to the shared helper. The one straggler,
`app/app/my-cv/actions.ts`'s `uploadMyCv()`, was still hand-rolling it - not exploitable today either
(both forms strip every `/`, confirmed: `safeFileName("../../etc/passwd")` and the inline regex both
produce a string with no `/` in it), but it was missing the shared helper's 120-char length cap and
its space/parenthesis allowance, exactly the drift the header comment predicted.

**Fixed:** `my-cv/actions.ts` now imports and calls `safeFileName()` instead of hand-rolling its own
regex - now identical to every other upload action in the app, and picking up the length cap for
free. Updated `safeFileName.ts`'s own header comment to record this sweep and retire the stale "~8
other files" count (re-grepped: zero stragglers remain after this fix).

**Verified for real:** added `lib/safeFileName.spec.ts` (the shared helper itself had no dedicated
test anywhere despite being security-relevant for 14 importers) - 4 checks: an ordinary filename
passes through unchanged, every `/`-or-`\` form is stripped (path traversal stays impossible), a
500-char name is capped at 120, and a genuinely-empty name (not merely all-separators, which still
sanitizes to a non-empty string) falls back to `"document"` - caught my own first draft of that last
check being wrong before running it (assumed `safeFileName("///")` falls back to `"document"`; it
doesn't, `"///"` sanitizes to `"___"`, which is truthy - fixed the test to assert the real behaviour
after checking directly with `node --experimental-strip-types`, not by guessing). `npx vitest run
lib/safeFileName.spec.ts`: 4/4 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean. `npx eslint app/my-cv/actions.ts
lib/safeFileName.spec.ts`: clean. Grepped all 14 importers of `safeFileName` to confirm the function
itself was unchanged (only `my-cv/actions.ts` gained a new caller) - no risk to the other 13.

## This pass (2026-11-03, standing solution-architect review): tried a real PDF decompression bomb against `requirements.pdf_text_or_error()` - genuinely already bounded, no fix needed

Oriented from `4353040` (the prior pass's own zip decompression-bomb fix on `collect_documents()`,
independently re-verified by Sarel's own session building a separate 400MB bomb by hand). `git fetch
origin main` found nothing newer; local already matched `origin/main`. Open PRs re-checked: only
`#164`/`#165` remain, both unchanged since 2026-10-26, no collision.

That pass's own technique - build a real adversarial input and run it through the real consumer,
not just reason about it - prompted trying the same document-bomb shape against a *different*
parser on the same intake path: `engine/general/requirements.py`'s `pdf_text_or_error()`, which
shells out to the real `pdftotext` (poppler) on every uploaded/downloaded PDF, with a 120-second
subprocess timeout already in place but no check on how much it decompresses or how much memory it
uses before that timeout fires.

Built two real PDF decompression bombs by hand (a minimal hand-rolled PDF: one `Flate`-compressed
content stream of millions of repeated `Tj` text-show operators, the same DEFLATE algorithm a zip
bomb exploits, since PDF content streams use it too):
- Bomb 1: a 495KB file whose content stream decompresses to 170MB (~343:1 ratio, 5,000,000 repeats).
  Ran the real `pdftotext` binary against it while polling `/proc/<pid>/status` for `VmRSS` every
  0.3s: finished in 4.5s, peak RSS **16.8MB** - nowhere near the 170MB decompressed size.
- Bomb 2: scaled 10x - a 4.9MB file decompressing to 1.7GB (50,000,000 repeats, same ratio). Finished
  in 48s (time scaling roughly linearly with decompressed size, confirming `pdftotext` genuinely
  processes the whole stream, not short-circuiting), peak RSS **1.8MB** - poppler is clearly
  streaming the Flate-decompressed content through its parser rather than buffering the whole thing
  in memory, the same architectural property that already defended the entity-amplification bomb a
  sibling pass tried against `.docx` parsing (libxml2's own internal cap, a different library, same
  shape of protection).

Net finding: a PDF decompression bomb against this specific call site cannot exhaust a worker's
memory (confirmed, not assumed, at two different scales) and cannot run longer than the 120-second
subprocess timeout the code already enforces - worst case is "one worker spends up to 120s on it,
then gets a clean `pdftotext timed out...` error," not the open-ended, no-limit-at-all disk-filling
shape the zip bomb had. Also worth noting for the record (not a vulnerability, just why the obvious
"repeat the same text many times" bomb shape produces small real output here): the exact repetition
that gives DEFLATE its high compression ratio is also what `pdftotext`'s own line-clustering logic
collapses into a handful of output lines, so this attack shape can't even produce a large captured
`stdout` to add a second risk on top - confirmed directly (8.3KB of output text from both bombs,
regardless of 170MB vs. 1.7GB of underlying decompressed content).

**No fix needed** - genuinely confirmed bounded by two independent mechanisms already in place
(poppler's own memory-safe streaming parse, and the function's existing subprocess timeout), not
assumed safe because nothing obviously bad happened. Did not pursue further exotic PDF attack shapes
(nested/chained filters, object-stream self-reference "quines") in this pass - noted as something a
future pass could try, not flagged as a known gap.

Committed docs-only (no code change - nothing to fix):
- `docs/specs/System-Status.md`

**Backlog: 19 → 19** (no new item, nothing resolved - this pass closed out an investigation with a
confirmed-clean result, it didn't find a standalone bug).

## This pass (2026-11-03, standing solution-architect review): `requirements.collect_documents()`'s zip unpacking had no decompression-bomb cap at all - a 200KB zip extracted to 200MB in just over a second, with nothing to stop a much bigger one - fixed

Oriented from `9bdcf55` (a sibling "standing QA/robustness review" pass's own clean sweep: a real
XML entity-amplification/"billion laughs" `.docx` built by hand and run against both real docx
consumers, neither vulnerable - libxml2's own built-in entity cap already defends it). `git fetch
origin main` found nothing newer; local fast-forwarded to match. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub
API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both unchanged since 2026-10-26, no collision.

That sibling pass's technique - build a real adversarial input and run it through a real consumer,
not just reason about it - prompted checking the other classic document-bomb shape against a
*different* parser: a zip-based decompression bomb (not an XML entity one) against
`engine/general/requirements.py`'s own zip unpacking in `collect_documents()` (ESKOM and other
sources publish tender packs as zips; this feeds both the general-pack builder and
`watch_tender_updates.py`'s own re-extraction of a changed pack).

First ruled out zip-slip (path traversal) two ways: confirmed CPython 3.13's own `zipfile`
`_extract_member()` already strips `..`/empty/`.`-only path components outright (read its actual
source: `invalid_path_parts = ('', os.path.curdir, os.path.pardir)`) - stdlib-safe by design,
nothing to fix there. `collect_documents()` *also* has its own explicit, independent zip-slip guard
(`os.path.realpath()` + a `startswith()` check) predating this pass - genuinely defended twice over,
confirmed clean.

Decompression bombs are a different attack surface entirely: built a real one by hand (a `.docx`
named zip entry filled with 200MB of zeros, `ZIP_DEFLATED` level 9) - **204KB on disk, ~1000:1 ratio**.
Ran it through the real `collect_documents()` directly: it extracted the full 200MB to disk in 1.2
seconds, with **no size check anywhere in the path** - not on the zip's own stated `file_size` header
(which a crafted zip can misstate to begin with, so checking it wouldn't even have been a real
guarantee), not during the actual streamed copy. A worker processing a hostile or merely corrupted
zip from any tender-document source had nothing stopping it from filling its own disk - affecting
every job sharing that worker, not just the one tender.

**Fixed:** `collect_documents()`'s zip-extraction loop now streams each member in 1MB chunks (never
trusting the header's stated size) and enforces two caps, checked live against bytes actually
written: `_ZIP_MEMBER_MAX_BYTES` (300MB per file - generous for a real drawing-heavy tender pack) and
`_ZIP_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES` (1GB per zip, summed across all its members - catches a "many small entries"
bomb that no single member would trip). Tripping either cap deletes the partial file, fires a
`system_alerts.record()` warning (same non-fatal pattern `read_document()`'s own OCR-crash handling
already uses two functions down), and marks that zip `unreadable` in the manifest rather than
crashing or silently claiming success - an ordinary small zip is completely unaffected.

**Verified for real, genuine red-then-green:**
- Built the 200MB-zero-byte bomb above by hand, ran it against the real pre-fix code: extracted in
  full, 209,715,200 bytes on disk, 1.2s, no warning of any kind.
- Built a second, 400MB bomb (over the per-member cap): post-fix, correctly stopped, 0 bytes left on
  disk, one `system_alerts.record()` warning fired, the zip entry marked `unreadable`.
- Built a third bomb from 9 separate 150MB members (1.35GB total, each individually under the
  per-member cap, to specifically test the *total* guard rather than the per-member one): post-fix,
  stopped after 6 members (900MB), never reaching the 7th - confirms the "many small entries" shape
  is caught too, not just one giant member.
- Added `test_requirements.py::check_zip_decompression_bomb_is_capped()` (4 new checks: the
  per-member cap, nothing left on disk after it trips, the total cap, and - the negative control - an
  entirely ordinary small zip still extracts normally, unaffected by either guard). Stashed just the
  `requirements.py` fix and re-ran: genuine red, all 4 new checks fail exactly as predicted (315MB and
  1.35GB land on disk with nothing flagged). Restored: genuine green, `0 failure(s)` across the whole
  suite (unchanged pre-existing tests included).
- `ast.parse` clean on both touched files. `ruff check` on both: 20 pre-existing findings total, none
  on any touched line (checked line-by-line against the diff - the new code is lines 132-207, every
  finding sits well outside that range).
- Confirmed `build_general_pack.py` (the real caller feeding a general pack) still imports and wires
  through cleanly with the new module-level constants in place.
- No live-database access, no mutation - pure Python extraction-loop fix, nothing SQL to replay.

Committed and pushed directly to `main` (small, fully verified, no PR):
- `engine/general/requirements.py`
- `engine/general/test_requirements.py`
- `docs/specs/System-Status.md`

**Backlog: 19 → 19** (standalone bug, now fixed - nothing added, nothing resolved from Sarel's own
judgment-call list. Worth a general observation for Sarel, not a backlog item: this is now the
*second* real "constructed adversarial input against a real parser" finding today, after the
entity-amplification one - both document-bomb classes checked, both now actually defended, one newly
so).

## This pass (2026-11-03, standing solution-architect review): DBSA re-broke its own closing-time format (`@` -> `at`), silently re-opening the exact 2026-10-29 bug - fixed, and confirmed it was actively showing already-closed RFPs as open

Oriented from `566d604`; `git fetch origin main` found nothing new, local already matched
`origin/main` exactly. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both
unchanged since 2026-10-26, no collision.

Per this pass's own rotation, tested a discovery scraper against its real live site rather than just
its fixture - picked `engine/discovery/dbsa_procurement.py` (last fixed 2026-10-29 for discarding
DBSA's own stated `@ 23H55` closing time; not live-tested since). Ran `fetch_releases()` against the
real `dbsa.org/procurement` page just now: **all 14 open RFPs came back with `closing_date: None`**.
Traced it to the raw HTML: DBSA's own page now writes `"13 November 2026 at 23H55"` - the separator
word changed from `@` to `at` sometime after the 2026-10-29 fix was verified, and `_AT_TIME`'s regex
only ever matched `@`, so `_parse_dbsa_closing()` fell through to `iso_sast_closing()` on the
un-stripped `"...at 23H55"` string, which `parse_sast()`'s strict `_DMY_DT` regex can't match -> `None`.
The exact same bug shape as 2026-10-29, re-introduced by the site itself, not by any code change here.

**Worse than a display glitch, confirmed live:** `source_http.is_past(None)` returns `False` ("unknown
is not expired"), and `is_closed = is_past(closing_date)` - so every DBSA RFP whose real deadline had
already passed was being reported `is_closed: False` and surfaced as a still-open opportunity. Direct
proof: re-running `fetch_releases()` after the fix below returned 12 open RFPs, not 14 - the 2 that
dropped out are ones whose real stated deadline (now correctly parsed) is already in the past.

**Fixed:** `_AT_TIME`'s regex now matches `@` OR `at` (`\s*(?:@|at)\s*(\d{1,2})H(\d{2})`, case-insensitive)
before the `H`/`MM` time, same conversion to `parse_sast()`'s `HH:MM` form as before. One row
(`RFP 200/2026`) still returns `None` - DBSA's own page has a literal typo there, `"23H555"` (an extra
digit), which no sane regex should guess at; same acceptable "unparseable -> unset, not a crash"
category the 2026-10-29 fixture already covers for a typo'd month.

**Verified for real:**
- Live: `_parse_dbsa_closing("13 November 2026 at 23H55")` -> `None` before the fix, `"2026-11-13T23:55:00+02:00"`
  after - genuine red-to-green confirmed by stashing the fix and re-running.
- Live: `fetch_releases()` against the real page now returns 12 open RFPs (down from the buggy 14),
  11 of 12 with a real parsed closing time, 1 (`RFP 200/2026`) correctly `None` from DBSA's own
  `"23H555"` typo.
- Added a dedicated `'at HH'H'MM'` fixture assertion to `test_gov_sources.py` alongside the existing
  `'@ HH'H'MM'` one (kept, in case DBSA reverts or mixes both). `python3 test_gov_sources.py` -> ALL
  PASSED. Adjacent sanity sweep: `test_source_http.py`, `test_tender_updates.py` - both clean.
  `py_compile` clean on both touched files.
- No live-database access, no mutation - pure code/parsing fix wired through `gov_sources.py`'s
  existing flow, nothing SQL to replay.

Committed and pushed directly to `main` (small, fully verified, no PR):
- `engine/discovery/dbsa_procurement.py`
- `engine/discovery/test_gov_sources.py`

## This pass (2026-11-03, standing solution-architect review): PayFast ITN handler never checked `amount_gross` - the 4th of PayFast's own documented ITN security checks, missing - fixed

Oriented from `477afe4`; `git fetch origin main` found nothing new, local already matched
`origin/main` exactly. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain (both
untouched since 2026-10-26), no collision with anything touched here.

Read `app/lib/billing.ts` (pricing/limits), then followed its only money-adjacent consumer that
hadn't had a dedicated pass yet: `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts` and `app/lib/payfast.ts`.
The route's own header comment claims "every one of PayFast's own documented ITN security checks is
done" and lists three: signature (`verifyItnSignature`), source IP (resolves against PayFast's
documented hostnames), and server confirmation (`eng/query/validate` returns `"VALID"`). Checked that
claim against PayFast's own published ITN security-check list (`payfast.kayako.com/article/321` -
"What causes the ITN security check errors?") rather than assuming it from the code: PayFast documents
a **fourth** check - that the ITN's `amount_gross` matches what your own records say this transaction
was for - described there explicitly as a real class of error ("amount mismatch... occurs when the ITN
amount differs from the amount your database holds for that transaction"). `apply_payfast_itn()`
(0078/0081/0082/0083/0110) never looked at an amount at all - a `COMPLETE` ITN that passed signature +
IP + server confirmation was applied at face value regardless of `amount_gross`, so the route's own
"every one... is done" claim wasn't true. Low exploit likelihood on its own (PayFast's outgoing
checkout amount is itself signed, so tampering it client-side breaks PayFast's own acceptance of the
transaction before it ever reaches our ITN) - but it's PayFast's own documented check, explicitly
named in their own troubleshooting of real ITN failures, and the gap was real and checkable, not
theoretical.

Fixed with a new migration, `0112_payfast_itn_amount_verification.sql`:
- `tt_plan_price_zar(plan_tier, billing_interval)` - a new SQL function mirroring `lib/billing.ts`'s
  `PLAN_MONTHLY_ZAR`/`priceForPlanZar()`/`yearlyPriceZar()` exactly, same "two copies, never imported
  across the app/database boundary" convention `tt_plan_limits()` (0083) already uses for
  `PLAN_LIMITS` - pricing itself still lives in exactly one real place (`lib/billing.ts`); this is only
  the read-only SQL-side mirror `apply_payfast_itn()` needs to verify an amount, never the other
  direction.
- `apply_payfast_itn()` gains a new `p_amount_gross numeric` parameter (old 4-arg signature dropped
  outright, not left granted alongside the new one). For any ITN that would activate a subscription
  (`COMPLETE`), it now looks up the plan/interval that specific `m_payment_id` was actually checked out
  for - `company_subscriptions`' own current row for the ordinary path, `payfast_payment_attempts`'
  append-only record (0081/0082) for the superseded-attempt rescue path - and raises (`P0003`, failing
  closed, same as every other ITN check) if `amount_gross` doesn't match that plan's price. A `FAILED`
  ITN activates nothing, so it's never gated on amount.
- `app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`: extracts `amount_gross` from the ITN body and passes it
  through to the RPC as `p_amount_gross` (`null` if absent/non-numeric, which the SQL side then
  correctly rejects for any `COMPLETE` ITN); header comment's "every one... is done" list now actually
  has 4 items, truthfully.

**Verified against a real Postgres, not just read**: started the local Postgres service, created a
disposable scratch database, and replayed the stub + all 102 real `app/supabase/migrations/*.sql`
files in order via `engine/security/replay_schema.sh` (clean - `== Schema replay complete (102
migrations) ==`, including this migration itself). Then, against that replayed schema, ran 5 concrete
scenarios by hand (`set role authenticated` + `test.uid`, same harness pattern
`test_tenant_isolation.py` uses): (1) a real `start_payfast_checkout('professional','monthly')`
followed by `apply_payfast_itn(...)` with a **wrong** `amount_gross` (R10 instead of R2,990) -
correctly raised `P0003` and left the row `trialing`, untouched; (2) the same `m_payment_id` with the
**correct** amount (R2,990) - correctly activated, `professional`, right limits; (3) a second checkout
(`business`/`yearly`) superseding the first on `company_subscriptions`, then the **rescue path**
(0081/0082) replayed for the superseded `professional`/`monthly` attempt with the **wrong** amount
(R4,990) - correctly raised `P0003`; (4) the same rescue with the **correct** amount (R2,990) -
correctly rescued the right company into `professional`/`monthly`/`active` with the right limits,
reclaiming `payfast_m_payment_id`, exactly matching 0082's own pre-existing documented behaviour; (5) a
`FAILED` ITN with `amount_gross` entirely absent (`null`) on a fresh company/attempt - correctly still
set `past_due` with `current_period_end` left `null`/untouched, confirming the amount gate never blocks
the one ITN type (`FAILED`) that was never meant to need one. `grep`-confirmed `apply_payfast_itn` has
exactly one real caller in the whole codebase (the route handler, now updated) - no other code needed
touching for the signature change. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npx vitest run lib/payfast.spec.ts
lib/billing.spec.ts` - 28/28 passed (both suites untouched by this fix, run to confirm no regression),
`eslint` clean on the touched route file. Scratch database dropped and the local Postgres service
stopped immediately after.

Committed and pushed directly to `main`:
- `app/supabase/migrations/0112_payfast_itn_amount_verification.sql` (new)
- `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts`
- `docs/specs/System-Status.md`

**Backlog: 18 → 19** (new item: migration `0112` needs applying to live DB, same as the other 6 - now
7 - pending migrations; nothing else changed or re-flagged).

clean-sweep entry for discovery rotation, no overlap) and fast-forwarded local `main` to match. Open
PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both unchanged, no collision.

Read `engine/worker/run_bridges.py` in full (245 lines) - the runner that drives all six bridges
(`cv`/`cv_extract`/`pack`/`general`/`onboarding`/`narrative`) every cycle in `--loop` mode (what the
container actually runs). Checked `resolve_bridge_names()`/`resolve_scripts()`'s additive-`--script`
interaction, the `_missing_reported` bookkeeping, and the timeout/process-group-kill path - all correct,
no bug there. Confirmed all six registered bridge scripts exist and support `--once`.

Found the real bug by comparing how each bridge reports an empty queue: `run_bridges.py`'s own
`QUIET_PREFIXES = ("No pending",)` exists specifically so a pass that finds nothing stays silent in
the log (its own comment: "In loop mode that would be two log lines every 30 seconds forever, burying
the ones that matter"). Five of the six bridges (`cv`, `cv_extract`, `pack`, `general`, `onboarding`)
print `"No pending ..."` on an empty queue, matching the prefix. `engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py`
- added only on 2026-10-25 to close the "narrative requests never got processed" gap - instead printed
`f"Processed {handled} job(s)."` unconditionally, even when `handled == 0`. `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_SECONDS`
is 30s, so the real worker logged `"narrative: Processed 0 job(s)."` every 30 seconds, forever, burying
real alerts under noise - exactly the failure mode `QUIET_PREFIXES` exists to prevent - and also
inflated `run_bridges.py`'s own "did something" activity count every single idle cycle.

Fixed in `engine/narrative/process_narrative_jobs.py`'s `main()`: prints `"No pending narrative document
requests."` when `handled == 0`, matching every sibling bridge's convention; unchanged
`"Processed N job(s)."` when `handled > 0`. Added a regression test
(`test_main_once_with_nothing_queued_prints_a_quiet_prefixed_line`, in
`engine/narrative/test_process_narrative_jobs.py`) that runs `main()` end-to-end against a stubbed-empty
queue and asserts the printed line starts with `"No pending"` - confirmed it fails against the
pre-fix code (`"Processed 0 job(s)."`) and passes against the fix. Full suite:
`python3 engine/narrative/test_process_narrative_jobs.py` -> `0 failure(s)` (13 tests, up from 12).

No new backlog item - a standalone, now-fixed log-noise bug, not a judgment call for Sarel. The 18-item

## Earlier pass (2026-11-02, standing solution-architect review): Market Intelligence's "By buyer" breakdown silently split SANRAL across two groups - the same real buyer, two different raw strings, no normalisation before grouping

Oriented from `8106221`; `git fetch origin main` found one new sibling commit (`e08f1ea`, docs-only
clean sweep of the intake rotation, no overlap) and fast-forwarded local `main` to match. Open PRs
re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both unchanged, no collision.

Picked `app/app/market-intelligence/page.tsx` + `app/lib/marketPricing.ts` - a fresh area, not yet
reviewed this session (the "market-wide overview" section, deliberately separate from `/analytics`'
company-scoped pricing trends). Read `marketPricing.ts` in full; found a real bug in `byBuyer()`.

`store_award_outcomes.py` writes the `buyer` column onto `public_tender_outcomes` from two different
raw strings for the exact same real-world buyer, SANRAL: `part_from_sanral()` hardcodes the literal
`"SANRAL"` when a tender is scraped from SANRAL's own site, while `part_from_portal()` stores eTenders'
own free-text `organ_of_State` value verbatim (a real captured sample: `"South African National Roads
Agency Soc Limited (SANRAL)"`). `outcome_key()`'s own `is_sanral_buyer()` already recognises both
strings as the same buyer - but only for MERGE purposes (combining the same tender seen from two
sources into one row); the merge's own `"buyer": first("buyer")` never canonicalises which string wins,
so a SANRAL tender known to this table ONLY via eTenders (never also scraped from SANRAL's own site -
entirely plausible; SANRAL's own site plainly doesn't claim to mirror every organ-of-State listing)
keeps the long eTenders string verbatim in the stored row. `byBuyer()` then grouped market-wide rows by
that raw, uncanonicalised string with no normalisation at all - silently splitting SANRAL, almost
certainly the single largest, most data-rich buyer in this whole backfilled ~39,500-row table, across
two (or more) separate rows on the live Market Intelligence "By buyer" table, each with a smaller, less
representative `n`/median/etc. than SANRAL's own real combined figures. The existing test's own
docstring ("groups by the exact buyer name") shows this was the file's actual, deliberate design at the
time it was written - not an oversight nobody considered, but written before this specific cross-source
SANRAL string variance was known; the module's own `normName()`/`is_sanral_buyer()` precedent for
bidder/winner names shows the authors already recognise and solve this exact "same real entity, two
raw strings" shape elsewhere in this same file, just not here.

Reproduced directly first: a standalone repro test with `buyer: "SANRAL"` and
`buyer: "South African National Roads Agency Soc Limited (SANRAL)"` confirmed `byBuyer()` returned 2
groups, not 1 (confirmed red). Fixed by adding `isSanralBuyer()` (a direct TS mirror of
`store_award_outcomes.is_sanral_buyer()`) and canonicalising the buyer key to `"SANRAL"` in
`groupBySingle()` whenever it matches, scoped narrowly to the one demonstrated case rather than a
sweeping generic buyer-name normaliser (which would risk merging genuinely different government
departments that happen to share a word) - `province` is left untouched, with no known equivalent
variance. Added 2 regression tests: the merge case (3 differently-spelled SANRAL rows -> 1 group of 3),
and a "doesn't over-merge" case (an unrelated buyer sharing the word "Agency" stays separate). Confirmed
red against the unfixed source via `git stash` (the merge test failed exactly as expected, the
non-merge test still passed), green after restoring.

Verification: `npx vitest run lib/marketPricing.spec.ts` -> 13/13 (up from 11); full `npx vitest run`
-> 337/337 (up from 335); `node --experimental-strip-types --test lib/*.test.ts` -> 215/215, unaffected
(sanity sweep, nothing in that family touches this file); `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` on both
touched files clean.

backfill needed):

Oriented from `7513108`; `git fetch origin main` found one new sibling commit (`b90b5e3`, a clean

The discovery-scraper-against-its-real-live-site streak has now covered essentially every scraper in
`engine/discovery/`, so this pass picked a different, not-yet-stress-tested parsing file:
`engine/intake/classify_tender.py` (the first thing that happens to a tender's documents on intake -
SANRAL/general routing, NRA reference, delivery address, closing time). The file already carries many
dated QA-pass comments (10-17 through 10-30) hardening its NRA/address/discrepancy logic against real
SANRAL text - read it end to end and stress-tested the regexes against constructed real-phrasing
variants rather than just reading the code.

**Found and fixed a real bug**: `CLOSING_TIME_RE`/`find_closing_time()` read the Tender Notice's own
"closing time ... is HH:MM" sentence, but never accounted for a 12-hour AM/PM suffix - `"2:00pm"` came
back as the literal digits `"02:00"` (2am), 12 hours wrong, with no conversion at all. Confirmed this
isn't a purely theoretical worry invented for this pass: `source_http.py`'s own `_US_DT`/`parse_sast()`
already has to do the identical AM/PM-to-24-hour conversion for Transnet's real "11/30/2026 3:00:00 PM"
dates - proof a 12-hour time is a real pattern SA government procurement text uses, even though every
real SANRAL closing-time sample seen so far (this file's own docstring, `Form-Field-Audit.md`) states
24-hour time with no AM/PM. Checked specifically for any real captured SANRAL AM/PM closing time before
treating this as confirmed vs. speculative - found none, but the fix itself is the exact same cheap,
already-proven conversion `source_http.py` already uses, so there was no real cost to closing this gap
proactively rather than waiting for a live incident, consistent with this file's own stated design
philosophy of refusing to let a silently-wrong value through (`find_nra_reference()`/
`find_delivery_address()` above exist for the identical reason).

adding an optional `([AP]M)?` group and applying the same `hh % 12 + (12 if PM else 0)` conversion
`source_http.py` already uses. A real 24-hour time with no AM/PM suffix (every sample seen so far) is
completely unaffected - verified the existing test suite's own 24-hour/multi-separator/ambiguity cases
all still pass unchanged. Added 5 new regression cases (2pm, 9am, the 12:00pm-is-noon and
12:00am-is-midnight edge cases, and a PM time + its 24-hour equivalent correctly recognised as the SAME
time, not `ambiguous=True`). Revert-and-confirm-red performed (`git stash` on the source file alone,
keeping the new test assertions): 3 of the 5 new checks failed exactly as expected against the unfixed
regex; restored to a clean pass after un-stashing.

## This pass (2026-11-01, standing solution-architect review): fix - eskom_bulletin.py's "award" classifier required a word boundary that Eskom's own real reference numbers don't have, showing 5 real awarded tenders as still open

Oriented from `6363fdc`; `git fetch origin main` found one new commit since - `76451fe`, a sibling
pass's real fix to `process_onboarding_jobs.py`'s stale-upload self-heal logic - no overlap, fast-
forwarded local `main` to match. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain,
both unchanged, no collision.

Continuing this session's "test a discovery scraper against its real live source site" technique
(now 4 real bugs found: `sars_procurement.py`, `vaal_central_water.py`, `lephalale.py`, and this
one). Picked `eskom_bulletin.py` (not tested this way this session) and fetched the real live
`GetTender` API directly (200, 290KB, 316 real bulletin entries - 180 tenders, 136 notices under
the old code).

**Found and fixed a real, customer-facing bug**: `classify()`'s `award` pattern was `r"\baward|..."` -
the leading `\b` requires a non-word character right before "award". Every other notice kind here
(`cancel`, `bidder`, `regre[tr]`, `validity`) already tolerates Eskom gluing the notice word directly
onto the preceding station code with zero separator ("MWP2524DXcancellatio", "CANCELLAE3122GXGPLET")
- `award` alone kept the boundary requirement, and Eskom glues its own award notices onto the
reference the exact same way ("E1828GXMPTUTaward", "E1635CXMWPAward" - "T" and "award" are both word
characters, so `\b` never matches). Confirmed against the real live data: **5 real bulletin entries
today** - `E1828GXMPTUTaward`, `E1859GXMPTUTaward`, `E2074GXMPTUTaward`, `E2232GXMPTUTaward`,
`E1635CXMWPAward` - are genuine award notices (every one's real `HEADER_DESC` ends in "... Award.")
with a real future `CLOSING_DATE`, misclassified as `"tender"` instead of `"award"`. Every one of
these would have been fed to Discovery with `status="advertised"` as if still open for bidding, when
the contract has already been awarded to someone else - a customer could have genuinely wasted real
time preparing a bid for work that's already gone.

Fixed by dropping the `\b` (matching the same no-boundary tolerance every sibling pattern already
has): `r"award|successful\s+bidder|intention\s+to\s+award"`. Verified precisely scoped before
committing - ran `classify()` against all 316 real live entries both before and after the change:
**exactly these 5 entries flip** `tender` → `award`, zero other entries change (no new false
positive from the wider match - checked specifically for any legitimate tender whose text merely
contains "award" as a substring elsewhere; none exists in the real live data today).

Added a new real-data regression case to `test_gov_sources.py`'s existing `ESKOM_NOTICES` list
(`E1828GXMPTUTaward`, the real `HEADER_DESC`, expected kind `award`, expected base reference
`E1828GXMPTUT`). Revert-and-confirm-red performed (`git stash` on the source file alone, test file
kept): `1 FAILED: classify E1828GXMPTUTaward (tender)` against the unfixed regex, restored clean -
`ALL PASSED` (the full `test_gov_sources.py` suite, unaffected elsewhere) - after. `py_compile` clean
on both touched files.

## This pass (2026-11-01, standing solution-architect review): fix - lephalale.py's TNUM_RE dropped a real T-number to None when it wrapped across two physical PDF table rows

Oriented from `79b8d69`; `git fetch origin main` found nothing new - local already matched
`origin/main` exactly. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both
unchanged, no collision.

Continuing this session's "test a discovery scraper's regex against its real live source site"
technique (which has now found real bugs in `sars_procurement.py` and `vaal_central_water.py`,
and confirmed `capetown_procurement.py`/`kouga.py` clean): `randwater.co.za` was unreachable this
pass (a TLS cert-chain problem on their own server, confirmed via the agent proxy's own status
endpoint showing no relay-level rejection - not pursued further per the standing rule against
disabling TLS verification). `lephalale.gov.za` was reachable; fetched its real live listing page
(332,919 bytes) and tested `ROW_RE` against it directly: 1117/1117 real `<tr>` rows matched
correctly, the other 6 `<tr>` blocks confirmed as legitimate header rows - that regex is clean.

Downloaded and `pdftotext -layout`'d the real, live "OCTOBER BATCH 23102026.pdf" (2 real tenders,
closing 09/11/2026 and 23/11/2026) and ran `parse_batch()` against the real extracted text.
**Found a real bug**: the second tender's own T-number, "T42/2025-2026(Re-Advert)" on the real PDF,
wraps across two physical table rows - `pdftotext -layout` emits "T42/2025-" at the end of one
output line (with that same row's OWN other column text, e.g. the description and enquiry-phone
columns, interleaved right after it on that same line), then "2026(Re-Advert)" at the very start of
the next output line. `TNUM_RE`'s old `-\s*(\d{4})` could only bridge whitespace, not the real words
sitting in between, so it matched nothing at all and this live, real tender's T-number silently came
back `None` - the exact "regex only tested against the one layout it happened to be written for"
shape this session has now found 3 times (`sars_procurement.py`'s attribute order,
`tender_enrichment.py`'s single-digit amounts, this).

Fixed by widening `TNUM_RE` with a second alternative that matches this exact wrap shape (end of
line, then the continuation at the very start of the next) without changing the first alternative at
all. Re-ran the new regex against the 3 existing real fixture PDFs (September/August/March) before
touching the source file - byte-for-byte identical T-numbers to the old regex in every case, so this

## This pass (2026-11-01, standing solution-architect review): fix - vaal_central_water.py's parser silently mangled a real "extension of validity" notice into a bogus tender with a reference number as its title, dropping 4 referenced tenders

Oriented from `ba3ac75`; `git fetch origin main` found nothing new since - local already matched
`origin/main` exactly. Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: only `#164`/`#165` remain, both
unchanged, no collision.

Continuing this session's technique of testing a discovery scraper's regex against its REAL LIVE
source site, not just the committed fixture: `kouga.py` checked clean (10/10 cards on page 1 matched,
`max_page()` correctly read 29 from the page's own pagination, no attribute-order variance found on
this site). `randwater.py`/`lephalale.py` were unreachable this pass (network timeouts through the
agent proxy, not a code issue - not pursued further).

**Found and fixed a real bug in `vaal_central_water.py`**, fetched live (122,951 bytes, 10 rows where
only 9 real tenders were expected from the module's own docstring). Row 1 was a real "EXTENSION OF
VALIDITY TO TENDERS" notice listing 5 separate reference numbers
(`VCW/MAINCE/25`/`VCW/MAINEB/25`/`VCW/MAINME/25`/`VCW383/LEGAL36/24`/`VCW261/PPE/21`) as 5 separate
`<p>` tags all crammed into the SAME widget `ROW_FIELDS` expects to hold exactly one reference, with
the real title ("EXTENSION OF VALIDITY TO TENDERS") sitting in the next widget, never reached.
`ROW_FIELDS`' own lazy `.*?` grabbed the second reference in that list as if it were the title,
producing a nonsense record (`ref="VCW/MAINCE/25"`, `title="VCW/MAINEB/25"`) and silently losing the
real title and the other 4 referenced tenders entirely - confirmed by direct comparison against a
normal row's HTML (ref and title each sit in their own single-`<p>` widget there).

Fixed by adding `_TITLE_LOOKS_LIKE_A_REFERENCE` (`^(?:VCW|BW)\S*/\d{2}$`) and skipping (with a logged
warning naming the dropped reference) any row whose "title" field is itself reference-shaped - a
genuine tender title never matches that pattern, so this reliably catches exactly the "my
one-reference-per-row assumption doesn't hold for this row" case without touching any real tender.
Threaded `log` through `parse_tenders()` (previously had no way to report a skip) from
`fetch_releases()`.

Verified: reproduced red first against the real live page (10 rows, row 0's bogus title confirmed);
after the fix, 9 rows (the exact 9 real references the module's own docstring names) plus one logged
warning naming `VCW/MAINCE/25`. Added a realistic fixture row (built from the real captured live HTML)
to `test_vaal_central_water.py`; confirmed it crashes against the unfixed source (`parse_tenders()` had
no `log` kwarg at all pre-fix - isolated the revert to just the source file via `git stash push --`,
keeping the new test assertions in place, rather than stashing both files together which would have
silently hidden the new checks and shown a false "ALL PASSED"). Full suite: `ALL PASSED` (26 checks,
up from 23); `test_gov_sources.py` sanity sweep unaffected; `py_compile` clean on both touched files.

This does NOT resolve the "extension of validity" notice's own real content (which tenders it extends,
to what date) - that information is now correctly dropped rather than corrupted, matching this
reader's existing no-notice-handling scope (unlike `eskom_bulletin.py`, this module has no concept of
a notice referring to other tenders - building that is a real feature, not a bug fix, and out of scope
here).

Committed and pushed directly to `main` (small, fully verified against the real live site, no live-DB
access needed):
- `engine/discovery/vaal_central_water.py`
- `engine/discovery/test_vaal_central_water.py`

GROUPS`/`formatZAR`/`pipeline` fixes, `tenderTemplates.ts` dual-list derivation, `generate_narrative.py`
similarity re-check) - all unrelated to this pass's own file, `git merge --ff-only` clean, no collision
(re-checked again immediately before pushing - still clean).

`daily_digest.py`'s JSON assembly.** Called `send_digest_emails.render_text()` directly with a real
`person_credential_before_closing` item and read the actual rendered line, rather than assuming Finding
139's own passing regression suite (which only exercises `daily_digest.py`, never the email body
itself) meant the full pipeline was correct end to end.

**The bug, confirmed live, predates Finding 139 entirely**: a `lapses_before_closing` item (both the
original `document_before_closing` shape, Finding 132, 2026-11-05, AND Finding 139's new
`person_credential_before_closing` shape) carries BOTH `expiry_date` (the document/credential's own
real lapse date - the one fact a reader needs, to know when to renew by) and `closing_date` (the
tender's) on the same item. `render_text()`'s `_item_date()` helper checks `closing_date` before
`expiry_date` in its priority order - correct for every OTHER section, which never sets both on one
item - so the generic trailing `(date)` this function always appended after its own custom "will have
lapsed before X closes (closing_date)" sentence silently resolved to `closing_date` again. Confirmed
directly: `SARS Tax Compliance Status PIN - will have lapsed before R.396-010-2025/1F closes
(2027-01-05) (2027-01-05)` - the same date twice, and the item's real `expiry_date` (`2027-01-15`)
never appearing in the sent email at all. Identical for the person-credential shape. Finding 139 didn't
introduce this - it only inherited the existing, already-live bug by correctly mirroring
`find_documents_lapsing_before_closing()`'s own item shape - but it does widen how often a real send
hits it (both the document and person-credential sections can now trigger it).

**Fix:** the sentence now names both dates explicitly (`"{label} (expires {expiry_date}) - will have
lapsed before {tender_label} closes ({closing_date})"`) and skips the generic trailing-date call for
this one branch, since both dates are already shown inline.

**Verified red-then-green.** New test covering both the document and person-credential shapes in
`test_send_digest_emails.py`, reverted the fix via `git apply -R` - failed exactly as predicted,
printing the real duplicated-date body; reapplied - `0 failure(s)`. `py_compile` clean. Regression:
`test_digest_live.py`, `test_send_pack_ready_email.py`, `test_digest_opt_in.py` - all `0 failure(s)`,

shape against the real send path, not a new or existing numbered judgment-call item.

## This pass (2026-11-05, standing QA/robustness review): fix - Eskom's own REFERENCE field truncates at 20 characters, cutting a glued notice word mid-word on real live bulletin entries; over a quarter of all real notices checked had a `refers_to_reference` that could never match any real tender

Oriented from `d44f7d1` (own prior pass: Finding 134, process_cv_jobs.py). `git fetch`/`merge --ff-only`
found one new sibling commit (`46f96ac` - re-verified my own Finding 134 fix closes the claim-outside-
try-block bug class across all 7 files, plus an `/experience` read; no overlap). Fast-forwarded cleanly.
Open PRs re-checked via the GitHub API: `#164`/`#165` only, both unchanged, no collision. Re-checked
again immediately before this push - still clean.

Rotated back to discovery (worker/job-queue was last, completing the full rotation once). Checked
findings-doc mention counts across every `engine/discovery/*.py` file; `eskom_bulletin.py` had zero
mentions. Read it in full (191 lines) and, since this is a live-scraped buyer feed with real network
access available in this environment, fetched the REAL live bulletin (322 entries) to check adversarial
cases against actual production data rather than constructed scenarios - this session's own standing
discipline (confirm against real data, as the intake/classify_tender.py rotation did last time with the
combined-SANRAL-forms hypothesis that got correctly ruled out for lack of evidence).

**Found and fixed Finding 135 (CONFIRMED, severe)**: `base_reference()` strips a glued notice word off a
notice entry's `REFERENCE` field so `tender_changes.py` can attach the notice to the real tender it's
about. Confirmed live: Eskom's `REFERENCE` field truncates at exactly 20 characters, so a glued notice
word that would push the combined string past that limit gets cut MID-WORD ("Validity" -> "Validit",
missing its own last letter; "Notification" -> "NOTIFICA", a word the list never had at all; plus the
list only ever had plural "names", never singular "name"). None of these truncated/missing fragments
matched the existing word list, so `base_reference()` fell through to returning the whole original
string - notice word and all - which then matches no real tender. Scanned all 139 real live notice
entries: **38 of them (over a quarter)** had a `refers_to_reference` that could never match anything,
silently orphaning the notice from the tender it was actually about.

**Fix:** added `"validit"` (ordered AFTER the full `"validity"` - Python's `re` tries alternatives left
to right and stops at the first match, not the longest, so order matters here), `"notifica"` (new), and
`"nameof"`/`"name"` (`"nameof"` before the shorter `"name"`, same ordering reason) to
`REF_NOTICE_WORDS`. Re-fetched the live bulletin after the fix: 38 of the 41 originally-broken cases now
resolve correctly. The remaining 3 have ZERO digits in their `REFERENCE` field at all (the real tender
reference lives only in `HEADER_DESC` text) - genuinely unfixable from `base_reference(ref)` alone since
it never receives the header; flagged as a smaller, separate, known gap rather than widening this fix to
chase it.

**Verified red-then-green.** Four new rows added to `test_gov_sources.py`'s own `ESKOM_NOTICES` fixture,
using the exact real `REFERENCE`/`HEADER_DESC` pairs from the live bulletin. Reverted the production
file alone: all four new checks failed exactly as predicted; restored: `ALL PASSED`. `py_compile` clean
on both files. Regression: `test_tender_updates.py`/`test_download_discovered_documents.py` both re-ran
clean.

Backlog: unchanged at 18 items - a contained data-quality fix, not one of Sarel's own 18 numbered
backlog items.
